usamts-2018-r2-01.title: Start from the tiny region
usamts-2018-r2-01.body:
Write $(r, c)$ for row $r$, column $c$. The region of area 1 is just the square marked 1 at $(5, 4)$, so its neighbours belong to other regions. The middle row reads $21, 19, 1, 13, 20, 19, 20, 19$, so the 19-region must reach $(5,3)$, $(5,7)$ and $(5,9)$ and also the marked squares $(2,5)$ and $(3,3)$, while the 20-region must reach $(5,6)$ and $(5,8)$ in between: the 19- and 20-regions have to interlock, the 19-region coming down from the top and the 20-region coming up from the bottom right. The 13-region must contain $(5,5)$, $(3,8)$ and $(7,8)$, and the 21-region the squares $(5,2)$, $(7,3)$ and $(8,6)$ on the left and bottom. Fitting these shapes with the exact areas gives
$$\begin{array}{cccccccccc} &  &  & 19 & 19 & 19 & 19 &  &  &  \\  & 21 & 21 & 19 & 19 & 13 & 19 & 19 & 19 &  \\ 21 & 21 & 19 & 19 & 13 & 13 & 13 & 13 & 19 & 20 \\ 21 & 21 & 19 & 13 & 13 & 20 & 19 & 19 & 19 & 20 \\ 21 & 21 & 19 & 1 & 13 & 20 & 19 & 20 & 19 & 20 \\ 21 & 21 & 21 & 21 & 13 & 20 & 20 & 20 & 20 & 20 \\ 21 & 21 & 21 & 21 & 13 & 13 & 13 & 13 & 20 & 20 \\  & 21 & 21 & 21 & 21 & 21 & 20 & 20 & 20 &  \\  &  &  & 20 & 20 & 20 & 20 &  &  & \end{array}$$

**Check.** Counting squares: region 1 has 1 square, region 13 has 13, region 19 has 19, region 20 has 20 and region 21 has 21 (total 74); each region is connected along gridlines, and every marked square lies in the region of its number (e.g. the 21 in row 8 is in the 21-region, the two 13's on the right in rows 3 and 7 are in the 13-region, which runs down column 5 and along rows 3 and 7).

**Answer: the partition above.**

usamts-2018-r2-02.title: Characterize $S$ by $\mathcal F(S)$
usamts-2018-r2-02.body:
For an unfriendly set $S$ we claim $S$ is exactly the set of *minimal* elements of $\mathcal F(S)$ under divisibility, i.e. the $m \in \mathcal F(S)$ with no proper divisor in $\mathcal F(S)$.

* If $s \in S$ had a proper divisor $m \in \mathcal F(S)$, then some $s' \in S$ divides $m$, hence divides $s$, with $s' \le m < s$: contradiction with unfriendliness. So elements of $S$ are minimal.
* If $m \in \mathcal F(S)$ is minimal, some $s \in S$ divides $m$, and $s \in \mathcal F(S)$; minimality forces $s = m$, so $m \in S$.

Thus $S$ is determined by $\mathcal F(S)$, and $\mathcal F(S_1) = \mathcal F(S_2)$ gives $S_1 = S_2$. ∎

usamts-2018-r2-03.title: Last chips and inclusion–exclusion
usamts-2018-r2-03.body:
Imagine Zan removes all 21 chips in a uniformly random order. Bob wins iff the last blue chip comes before both the last red chip and the last green chip. Let $E_R$ = "last blue before last red", $E_G$ = "last blue before last green"; we want $P(E_R \cap E_G) = P(E_R) + P(E_G) - P(E_R \cup E_G)$.

* $E_R$ happens iff, among the 13 red and blue chips, the one removed last is red: by symmetry each of the 13 is equally likely to be last, so $P(E_R) = \frac{6}{13}$.
* Similarly $P(E_G) = \frac{8}{15}$.
* $E_R \cup E_G$ fails only if the last blue chip comes after the last red and the last green, i.e. the very last of all 21 chips is blue: probability $\frac{7}{21} = \frac13$. So $P(E_R \cup E_G) = \frac23$.

Hence
$$P(\text{Bob wins}) = \frac{6}{13} + \frac{8}{15} - \frac23 = \frac{90 + 104 - 130}{195} = \frac{64}{195} \approx 32.8\%.$$

**Answer: $\frac{64}{195}$**

usamts-2018-r2-03.title: Recursion check
usamts-2018-r2-03.body:
Let $P(r, b, g)$ be Bob's winning probability with $r, b, g$ chips of each color left in the bag. Then $P(r, 0, g) = 1$ for $r, g > 0$, $P(0, b, g) = P(r, b, 0) = 0$ for $b > 0$, and
$$P(r, b, g) = \frac{r\,P(r-1,b,g) + b\,P(r,b-1,g) + g\,P(r,b,g-1)}{r+b+g}.$$
Evaluating exactly (by computer, with fractions) gives $P(6, 7, 8) = \frac{64}{195}$.

**Answer: $\frac{64}{195}$**

usamts-2018-r2-04.title: Compare roots of polynomials
usamts-2018-r2-04.body:
Treat $\binom xk = \frac{x(x-1)\cdots(x-k+1)}{k!}$ as a polynomial in $x$. Both sides are polynomials in $n$ that agree for infinitely many $n$, so they are identical.

**$a = 1$ or $b = 1$ fail.** If $a = 1$ the identity is $\binom nb = r\binom{n+s}{t}$; comparing degrees, $t = b$, and then for integers $n > b$, $\binom nb < \binom{n+s}{b} \le r\binom{n+s}{b}$ since $s \ge 1$. If $b = 1$ it reads $\binom na = r\binom{n+s}t$, and the same argument applies. So $a, b \ge 2$.

**Roots.** The right side $\frac{r}{t!}(n+s)(n+s-1)\cdots(n+s-t+1)$ has $t$ distinct integer roots. The left side is $\frac{1}{b!}\prod_{i=0}^{b-1}\left(\binom na - i\right)$, so every polynomial $\binom na - i$ ($0 \le i \le b-1$, each of degree $a$) must have $a$ distinct integer roots.

Which integers $n$ satisfy $\binom na = 1$? For $0 \le n \le a-1$, $\binom na = 0$; $\binom aa = 1$; for $n \ge a+1$, $\binom na \ge a + 1 \ge 3$. For negative $n$, $\binom na = (-1)^a\binom{a-1-n}{a}$ with $a - 1 - n \ge a$, which has absolute value 1 only for $n = -1$. So $\binom na - 1$ has at most two integer roots, forcing $a \le 2$, i.e. $a = 2$. Then $\binom n2 = 2$ means $n(n-1) = 4$, which has no integer roots, so $i = 2$ cannot occur: $b \le 2$, i.e. $b = 2$.

**$(2, 2)$ works:**
$$\binom{\binom n2}{2} = \frac12\cdot\frac{n(n-1)}2\left(\frac{n(n-1)}2 - 1\right) = \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)(n+1)}{8} = 3\binom{n+1}{4},$$
so $r = 3$, $s = 1$, $t = 4$. (Check $n = 4$: $\binom62 = 15 = 3\binom54$.)

**Answer: $(a, b) = (2, 2)$**

usamts-2018-r2-05.title: Radical center and Simson line (official idea)
usamts-2018-r2-05.body:
Let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$; by hypothesis $D$ lies on line $XY$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle, $\omega_B$ the circle with diameter $BH$ and $\omega_C$ the circle with diameter $CH$. Since $\angle BDH = \angle BXH = 90^\circ$, both $D, X \in \omega_B$; similarly $D, Y \in \omega_C$. Both $\omega_B$ and $\omega_C$ pass through $H$ and $D$.

**Step 1: $R = BX \cap CY$ lies on $AD$.** The radical axes of the pairs $(\omega, \omega_B)$, $(\omega, \omega_C)$, $(\omega_B, \omega_C)$ are the lines $BX$, $CY$, $HD = AD$. They are concurrent or all parallel. If they were parallel, then $BX \perp BC$ and $CY \perp BC$, so $X, Y$ would be the antipodes of $C, B$ and $XY$ would be parallel to $BC$, contradicting that $XY$ meets $BC$. So $R = BX \cap CY$ exists and lies on line $AD$. Also $R \ne D$ (else $X$ would lie on line $BC$).

**Step 2: $R$ is the reflection $A'$ of $A$ in $BC$.** $D, X, Y$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $H$ to the lines $BC$, $BR$, $CR$ (as $\angle HXB = \angle HYC = 90^\circ$). They are collinear, so by the converse of the Simson line theorem $H$ lies on the circumcircle of $BCR$. The circle through $B, C, H$ is the reflection of $\omega$ in $BC$ (because the reflection $S$ of $H$ in $BC$ lies on $\omega$ — a well-known fact). That circle meets line $AD$ exactly at $H$ and at $A'$, the reflections of $S$ and $A$. $R \neq H$ (a line $BX$ through $H$ cannot make $\angle BXH = 90^\circ$ with $X \ne H$ on it), so $R = A'$ and $RD = AD$.

**Step 3: lengths on line $AD$.** $S$ (the second intersection of $AD$ with $\omega$) satisfies $DS = DH$. Power of $R$: with respect to $\omega$, $RS\cdot RA = RB\cdot RX$; with respect to $\omega_B$, $RB\cdot RX = RD\cdot RH$. Hence $RS\cdot RA = RD\cdot RH$, and as $RA = 2RD$, $RH = 2RS$. Writing $h = DH = DS$ and $m = RD$: $RS = m - h$ and $RH = m + h$, so $m + h = 2(m - h)$, $m = 3h$. Then $AH = AD - DH = 3h - h = 2h$ and $HS = 2h$, so $H$ is the midpoint of the chord $AS$ of $\omega$.

**Conclusion.** $H \ne O$ (the triangle is not equilateral), and the segment from the center to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord: $OH \perp AS$. Since $AS \perp BC$, $OH \parallel BC$. ∎

(A numerical check over families of acute triangles confirms that $XY$ passes through $D$ exactly when the heights of $O$ and $H$ above $BC$ coincide.)
